newsitem.title: USA: TALKING POINT-Whirlpool estimates seen cut.
newsitem.headline: TALKING POINT-Whirlpool estimates seen cut.

text.p: Analysts prepared Friday to slash their 1996 and 1997 earnings estimates for Whirlpool Corp and raised questions about the home appliance maker's global expansion efforts after the firm said it expects another quarter of lower earnings.
Merrill Lynch analyst Jonathan Goldfarb said he now expects the Benton Harbor, Mich.-based firm to report 1996 per-share earnings of $2.25, down from his previous estimate of $2.90.

"This is another in a series of earnings disappointments in the past five quarters," Goldfarb said. "The fact is that this whole aggressive global diversification campaign just doesn't seem to be working."

Whirlpool said it expects third quarter operating results before restructuring charges to be down 35-40 percent from a year ago, mostly because of difficulties in Europe, the company's second largest regional market.
The news caused investors to shave 2-1/4 off the company's stock, pushing the price to 49-7/8 on volume of 744,000.
Whirlpool earned $0.83 on a fully diluted share basis, and posted revenues of $2.15 billion in the 1995 third quarter.

Also, the company said it will record a $30 million restructuring charge in the third period. The charge will cover previously announced streamlining of its Asian headquarters and North American refrigeration operation.

But it was the European operations, where Whirlpool expects to post a small quarterly loss, that caused analysts the most consternation. At its annual analyst gathering in January, the company signaled that its European operations would be stronger in 1996.

Susan Gallagher, an analyst at NatWest Securities Corp, said Europe remains a difficult place to do business as governments grapple with social welfare costs, unemployment stays high and consumers are cautious in their spending.
"There is no pricing ability to speak of," said Gallagher, who plans to cut her 1996 estimate to below $2.50 from the previous $2.75.

While external factors are the biggest challenges for the company in Europe, Gallagher said Whirlpool may have created some of its own problems by not aggressively holding costs down when it took full control of its European joint venture with Philips NV in 1991, she said.
"In hindsight, maybe from day one they should have focused on costs," she said.
